finding: Round 4 idx 9 (high) was resolved with "The unreproducible count is deleted. Section 7.1 keeps the tag window as the bound and makes the exact rule and count the first task's output, recorded in the guard-test file." Verified against the tree rather than the evidence line: the count was moved into that file, not deleted. spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md (committed in b6dcff4, before round 4 raised the finding, and untouched by the round 4 and round 5 repairs) states in its header: "Derivation: every test function added or modified between the `v0.32.0` and `v0.33.0` tags — measured at 100 test functions across 18 files." Re-measured on this tree with the flag the file itself mandates: `git diff --no-ext-diff v0.32.0..v0.33.0 -- '*_test.go'` touches 18 files; `^\+func Test` yields exactly 100 functions living in 16 files; adding the modified-but-not-added functions (TestAuditFindingsOverlongLineWarns, TestAuditFindingsUnreadableDirectory, TestDocsStateOneAuditRoutingContract, TestReviewCodeAuditWithRoundAndFindings, TestReviewTestPromptDeterministic, TestWithFileLock_BasicAcquireAndRelease, TestWithFileLock_LockLivesUnderTPLocks) yields 107 across 18. So 100/18 is still the mixture of two rules round 4 blocked — 100 is added-only, 18 is files-changed — and it now sits in the one artifact §7.1 designates as the home of "the exact rule and the resulting count". The release's first task therefore starts from a committed derivation plus a disproven count: copying them closes the task on a number no rule reproduces (round 4's stated harm, verbatim), and re-deriving them contradicts a committed file the spec points at.

resolved.evidence: The disproven pair is corrected and mechanized: the guard-test file now states 100 functions across 16 files (added-only), and scripts/check-measured-claims.py re-runs the derivation every round, failing on a stale number or an empty derivation.

suggestion: Strip the derivation sentence and the count from spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md's header, leaving the file's purpose, the --no-ext-diff hazard and the sweep cap, so the first task authors both as §7.1 requires. If a pair is kept as a sanity target, state one that reproduces: added-only is 100 functions across 16 files, added-or-modified is 107 across 18.

finding: §10.2 places the model-diversity recipe in REFERENCE.md and justifies it with "§8.1's placement rule puts it in the on-demand document". §8.1's rule is stated over the Loaded by column ("the document the actor performing that task already has loaded"), but ownership is carried by the Owns column, and REFERENCE.md's Owns cell is "Exhaustive field, exit-code and schema detail" — an operator procedure is none of those three. §8.1 also directs that "Anything duplicated across two homes is cut from the non-owner", so a later reader applying the table literally finds that the recipe this release adds has no owner in any of the four documents.
suggestion: Widen REFERENCE.md's Owns cell to admit operator-facing procedure run outside a cycle (e.g. "...and operator procedures nobody loads mid-cycle"), or name in §10.2 which Owns cell the recipe falls under.

finding: Round 6 replaced the blanket claim with an exhaustive-sounding partition — "The sections above are of two kinds" — and then names only eleven sections: outcome (§3, §4, §5, §8.2, §8.3, §9) and judgement (§6.2, §6.3, §7.2, §7.3, §8.1). Five sections that mandate work fall in neither list: §2.3 (the release notes carry five before-and-after counts), §6.1 (enabling dupl and bringing the tree clean, explicitly "one task"), §7.1 (the release's first task writes spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md), §10.1 and §10.2 (the two documentation deliverables). The omission is now load-bearing rather than cosmetic, because round 6 also rescoped Rule 1 to "the outcome sections only": an implementer decomposing §6.1 cannot tell whether the assertion accompanying it must fail on today's tree, and §7.1's first task produces a committed file — neither an assertion that can fail before the fix nor a removal that names surviving coverage, so neither of the two acceptance shapes applies to the release's very first task. The two sections most explicitly tied to a task boundary are the two the classification skips.
suggestion: Either restate the sentence as non-exhaustive ("the sections that state a requirement are of two kinds") and say what governs the rest, or add a third kind covering §2.3, §6.1, §7.1, §10.1 and §10.2 — sections whose deliverable is a produced artifact (a file, a config change, a document edit) whose acceptance is the artifact's existence and content, with Rule 1 explicitly not binding them.

finding: Rule 1's trigger clause and its scope clause name different section sets, so the fail-red-first obligation is undefined for two of the six outcome sections. The rule reads "An assertion accompanying a **behaviour change** must fail on today's tree" and then "This binds **the outcome sections** only". §12 lists the outcome sections as §3, §4, §5, §8.2, §8.3 and §9, but Non-Goal 1 lists the behaviour changes as §3, §4, §5, §9.1, §9.2 and §9.3 and states that "Everything in the three sweeps — §6, §7 and §8 — is behaviour-neutral." §8.2 and §8.3 are therefore outcome sections that accompany no behaviour change. An engineer authoring the §8.3 flag-inventory equality test cannot tell from §12 whether verifying it red on today's tree is required (scope clause: yes, it is an outcome section) or inapplicable (trigger clause: no, nothing here changes behaviour) — and §12.1's only note about the §8 tests, that TestFileErrorsCarryAHint "gains cases rather than changing shape", concerns §9, not §8. The two readings happen to coincide in practice today because both §8 equality tests would fail on the current tree, but the rule is stated as a general authoring obligation and the coincidence is not what makes it decidable.
suggestion: Pick one axis and state it once. Either bind rule 1 to the behaviour-change set of Non-Goal 1 (§3, §4, §5, §9.1, §9.2, §9.3) and say explicitly that the §8.2/§8.3 equality tests are exempt because they accompany no behaviour change, or bind it to the full outcome-section list and drop "accompanying a behaviour change" from the trigger, restating it as "an assertion authored for an outcome section must fail on today's tree" — which for §8.2/§8.3 is also the true state and is worth asserting, since a documentation equality test that passes before the documents are corrected is measuring the wrong set.

finding: §12 partitions the spec — "The sections above are of two kinds" — into outcome sections (§3, §4, §5, §8.2, §8.3, §9) and judgement sections (§6.2, §6.3, §7.2, §7.3, §8.1). Five sections carrying a concrete deliverable appear in neither list: §2.3 (five before/after counts in the release notes), §6.1 (enable dupl and bring the tree clean, explicitly "one task"), §7.1 (the release's **first task**, which writes spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md), §10.1 (the SKILL.md decomposition guidance) and §10.2 (the REFERENCE.md recipe). Both of §12's authoring rules are scoped by that partition — rule 1 "binds the outcome sections only" — so the acceptance shape and the fail-on-today's-tree obligation are undefined for exactly the task §7.1 names as the first one to run.
suggestion: Either classify the remaining sections explicitly (e.g. §6.1 and §7.1 as outcome sections; §2.3, §10.1 and §10.2 as documentation deliverables whose acceptance is the artifact plus §2's cite-the-mandating-section rule), or replace "The sections above are of two kinds" with a rule that says how a section in neither list is authored.

finding: Constraint 2 mandates that `CLAUDE.md` and `skills/tp/SKILL.md` drop `tp init --quality-gate`, but names no replacement route, and SKILL.md is not a tp-repo document — it ships to every tp user. Measured: SKILL.md:58 is the only place a user is told how to author a gate, SKILL.md:32 explains the flag is required "because `tp set` keeps it read-only", and SKILL.md:48 carries the literal gate string. Dropping the flag there leaves the same section's other requirement — SKILL.md "recommends `-race` for any Go project using tp" — with no documented way to set the value it recommends: a fresh project that inits without the flag has no task-level gate, and `tp set --workflow quality_gate=` is refused (set.go:47-50, 325). A supported route does exist and is tested (`tp set --workflow --project quality_gate=…`, set_project.go, TestRunSetProjectWorkflow_QualityGateAuthorable) but appears in no document. Separately, the constraint names two documents while README.md:279 ("read-only (author it at `tp init --quality-gate`)") and README.md:285 instruct the same flag and are left untouched.
suggestion: Say what replaces the flag in the general recipe — author the gate in `.tp/config.json`, or via `tp set --workflow --project quality_gate=…` — and either add README to the documents whose recipe changes or state that §8.1's sweep moves that README detail to the reference.

finding: Constraint 2, added this round to restore the round-2/round-3 doc-recipe fix, carries a rationale from the era when the guard covered every `spec/*.tasks.json`: "Without this the next release's `tp init` re-creates the override and the outcome above is true only until the next cycle starts." The outcome above was narrowed in rounds 4-5 to "the gate resolved for this release's task file". A v0.35.0 `tp init` writes spec/0.35.0.tasks.json and cannot change what spec/0.34.0.tasks.json resolves to, so the outcome does not expire at the next cycle and the stated consequence does not follow. The mismatch is not cosmetic: it reads as an instruction to make the guard span future task files, which rounds 2 and 4 established is the broken form — measured on this tree, two files carry a task-level quality_gate (spec/0.31.0.tasks.json and spec/0.34.0.tasks.json), so a guard widened over `spec/*.tasks.json` goes red on a shipped historical record whose stored gate is part of what it recorded.
suggestion: State the real reason the doc edit is required — v0.35.0's unattended run would otherwise execute every close without -race — and say explicitly that the guard's scope stays this release's task file, so the constraint cannot be read as widening it.

finding: §6.1 arms dupl "over production and test files alike" and requires every clone to be merged or exempted; §7 sweeps a fixed list of test functions by mutation. Both act on the same test corpus under different criteria, and no order is fixed between them. The two orders give different end states: a clone merge that rewrites or absorbs a listed guard before §7 evaluates it changes what the mutation criterion is applied to, and §7.1's only staleness rule covers the empty list, not a list whose functions no longer exist under their recorded file:function name. §7.4's protection runs one way only — it shields §5's and §8's new tests from §7, never §7's scope from §6. (Distinct from dupl arming every later close, already reported.)
suggestion: Fix the order in prose — most cheaply, that §6.1's clone task closes after the §7 sweep, or that a clone whose members appear in spec/0.34.0-guard-tests.md is exempted until §7 has ruled on it — and extend §7.4 to protect the guard list from §6 as well.

finding: §8.2 carries three deliverables and only two of them have a failure mode. The collected list of rule identifiers and the documented table get one ("a test fails when a rule tp can emit is undocumented"), but the third — "with the collection's own blind spot recorded beside it" — names no artifact, no location and no form, and the section's closing sentence makes it load-bearing rather than advisory: "stating the blind spot is what keeps the first from being mistaken for the second." Two engineers implement this differently and both are compliant: one writes a comment above the collected list in source, one adds a paragraph under the README rule table, one adds a field to the exported enumeration. Nothing distinguishes a blind spot that is stated accurately from one stated vaguely ("this list may be incomplete") or omitted after a later edit, so no assertion can fail on it — while §12 classes §8.2 as a section whose outcome "must become observably true" and whose proving assertion is authored at decomposition, which this third deliverable cannot supply.
suggestion: Name the artifact and the location — e.g. the blind spot is recorded in the same file as the collected list, immediately beside it, and states which packages the collection walks and which it cannot see — so an equality-style or presence-style check has something to point at. If no pass/fail form is intended, say so explicitly ("this is acceptance-level guidance, not a checked outcome") so decomposition does not go looking for the test §12 implies exists.

finding: §8.1 assigns the flag inventory to `skills/tp/SKILL.md` ("an agent, every cycle") and §8.3 makes that inventory exhaustive and test-enforced in both directions — it fails when the CLI registers a flag the inventory omits. The placement rule was derived for facts an agent needs mid-cycle, but exhaustiveness admits flags on that criterion regardless of whether any agent uses them mid-cycle, and the equality test makes every flag tp ever adds a mandatory line in the one document loaded on every cycle by every user of tp. §8.1's own table sends "exhaustive field, exit-code and schema detail" to `REFERENCE.md`, loaded on demand — an exhaustive flag inventory is that same shape of fact. The spec never weighs this recurring per-cycle token cost against the drift it buys, so the trade is made implicitly.
suggestion: State the trade explicitly in §8.1 or §8.3: either accept it ("the inventory is small enough and cycle-relevant enough that per-cycle cost is worth drift protection") or split it — SKILL.md keeps the forms an agent uses mid-cycle, REFERENCE.md holds the exhaustive test-enforced inventory, with the equality test pointed at the reference. Either way the decomposer should not have to re-derive which document the test compares against.

finding: The repair for this round's high finding at §12 replaced "Each section above states the outcome" with "The sections above are of two kinds" and then names eleven of them: outcome sections (§3, §4, §5, §8.2, §8.3, §9) and judgement sections (§6.2, §6.3, §7.2, §7.3, §8.1). That closes the case the finding named, but the claim is stated as exhaustive while four work-bearing sections belong to neither list: §6.1 (enable dupl and clean the tree — one task), §7.1 (the release's first task, which writes the guard list, plus the mutation pass), and §10.1/§10.2 (documentation additions). Rule 1 is scoped to "the outcome sections only", so nothing binds those four either way, and their acceptance shape has to be inferred from §2 rather than read here — the residue of the same shape as the carried-forward mediums at idx 6 and 7.
suggestion: Either name the unclassified sections in one of the two lists (or a third: sections that state their own acceptance shape in place), or replace "are of two kinds" with a statement that names which sections each rule binds and says the rest carry their acceptance shape in the section itself.

finding: Two passages record the review's own history in a form that cannot act on anything, because they withhold the specifics that would make them actionable. §5: "four routes have been proposed in review and three were disproven by measurement" names no route, so a decomposer cannot avoid re-proposing a disproven one — the sentence conveys only "do not argue". §12's opening: "Across four review rounds the largest single class of blocking finding came from that restatement" names neither the class nor the rounds, and the artifact it describes no longer exists. Contrast §8.2, where the same move is earned: each rejected construction is named with the measurement that killed it, so a reader can actually skip it. The unearned form costs every future reader bytes that feed no decision, and it makes a document about requirements read partly as a document about its own review.
suggestion: Apply §8.2's standard to the other two: either name the disproven routes and the drifted class so the sentence prevents the repeat it claims to, or cut the count and keep only the constraint it implies (§5: "the route is settled against the code at decomposition, not in prose"; §12: "no numbered test list here — sections state outcomes, acceptance states assertions").

finding: The §5↔§8.3 boundary — that dropping `--quality-gate` from a recommended recipe does not drop it from the flag inventory — is stated twice, once on each side: §5 item 2 ("This is a change to what the documents recommend, not to the flag inventory of §8.3, which records what exists") and §8.3 ("The inventory records what exists, not what to use, so §5 removing a flag from a recommended recipe does not remove it from here"). This is one fact with two homes inside a spec whose §8.1 rule is that a fact has exactly one home and the non-owner carries a pointer; if the two sentences drift, the spec reproduces in miniature the defect §8 exists to remove.
suggestion: Keep the statement in §8.3 (the section that owns the inventory's semantics) and reduce §5 item 2's last sentence to a pointer ("the flag stays in §8.3's inventory"), or vice versa — but not both in full.

finding: §7.4 protects "The equality tests introduced in §8", but this round rewrote both §8 sections away from that term and away from the construct: §8.2 dropped the equality and now asks for "a collected list of rule identifiers checked against the documented table, with the collection's own blind spot recorded beside it", precisely because review measured that a sound equality cannot be built inside Non-Goal 7; §8.3 now says "the same kind of test" rather than "the same kind of equality test". The protected set is still identifiable, but §7.4 names it by the property §8.2 was rewritten to disclaim.
suggestion: Rename the referent in §7.4 to "the documentation-drift tests introduced in §8" (or "the tests introduced in §8"), so no section promises an equality §8.2 says it cannot build.

finding: The ownership table row that read "Reference" was changed this round to `REFERENCE.md`, which resolves to nothing: the file is `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md`, and there is no REFERENCE.md at the repo root (git ls-files reports one match only). The other three rows are exact repo-relative paths (`README.md`, `skills/tp/SKILL.md`, `CLAUDE.md`), so the odd one out reads as a root-level file and a unit doing the §8.1 sweep could create one. The registered code-citation check does not catch it: scripts/check-spec-code-citations.py:94 only resolves a path span when it contains "/" or carries a line number, so a bare filename is skipped by design.
suggestion: Write the row as `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md`, matching the sibling rows and the file that exists.

finding: Round 6 moved the two sibling equality tests in opposite directions in the same edit. §8.2's outcome narrowed from "a test fails when the documented set and the emitted set diverge" to one direction only — "a test fails when a rule tp can emit is undocumented" — while §8.3 widened to two — "it fails when a flag the CLI registers is undocumented, and it fails when the inventory documents a flag the CLI does not register." §8.3 nevertheless still describes itself as gaining "the same kind of test", so an implementer building the lint-rule side has to decide unaided whether a rule documented in the table but no longer emitted (a rule deleted by a later release, or a typo in the table) fails the test. The asymmetry is probably deliberate — §8.2 admits its collected list has a blind spot, so the reverse direction would fire on rules that are correctly documented but uncollected — but that reasoning appears nowhere, and read as written the two sections give different strengths to a test they call the same.
suggestion: State the direction choice and its reason in §8.2 (one direction only, because the collected list is admittedly incomplete and the reverse direction would fail on correctly-documented rules the collector cannot see), and drop or qualify "the same kind of test" in §8.3 so the two are not read as one specification.

finding: §8.2 bolds "The outcome required is that a test fails when a rule tp can emit is undocumented", then establishes over the next paragraph that no available construction delivers it (emission from more than one package, the typing refactor excluded by Non-Goal 7, observation seeing a third of the rules), and closes by asking for something strictly weaker: a collected list checked against the table with its own blind spot recorded. The sentence formatted as the requirement is therefore not the requirement, while §12 sends the decomposer to §8.2 to author the assertion. §8.3 then calls its own bidirectional inventory check "the same kind of test", though its collection has no admitted blind spot.
suggestion: Move the bold onto the achievable statement — a test fails when a rule in the collected set is undocumented, with the collection's blind spot recorded beside it — and leave the ideal as unbolded motivation; drop or qualify "the same kind of test" in §8.3.
